body_markdown:
Swedish death cleaning, or *döstädning* , may have one of the most intimidating names in home organization. But the actual practice is much gentler than it sounds.


At its heart, Swedish death cleaning is a chance to look around your home and ask a few simple questions: Why do I have three bottle openers? Am I really going to sort this box of mystery cords? Would anyone besides me understand the significance of this souvenir cup?


Swedish death cleaning is a gradual way to sort through your belongings, keep the things that still belong in your life, and pass along what doesn’t before someone else has to organize it someday. It can be thoughtful, nostalgic, and practical.


## Quick Takeaways


- Swedish death cleaning is a[gradual decluttering](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/organizing/decluttering-when-youre-overwhelmed-low-effort-systems-that-stick.html) practice, not a one-weekend project.
- It focuses on keeping belongings that fit your life now and letting go of excess over time.
- The practice can work during a move, home update, downsizing project, or any time rooms and closets feel too full.
- The goal isn’t an empty home or strict minimalism.
- Starting with ordinary categories, such as duplicate kitchen tools and old cables, makes the process easier to begin.


## What Is Swedish Death Cleaning?


Swedish death cleaning is the practice of reviewing your belongings over time and deciding what still has a place in your home. The idea is to make those choices yourself rather than leaving every drawer, box, and shelf for someone else to sort through later.


The Swedish word *döstädning* combines *dö* , meaning death, and *städning* , meaning cleaning. While the name is direct, the process can be surprisingly comforting.


Author Margareta Magnusson introduced many readers to the concept in her book, *The Gentle Art of Swedish Death Cleaning* . Her approach isn’t about living with nothing. You can keep the books you reread, art you enjoy, photos that make you smile, and hobby supplies you’re still excited to use.


It’s about saving the people close to you from sorting through a[lifetime of accumulated belongings](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/moving/help-ive-inherited-a-hoarder-house-what-should-you-do-first.html) while making your home easier to enjoy now.


## Why Try Swedish Death Cleaning?


Swedish death cleaning gives decluttering a more personal purpose than simply “getting organized.”


It can be a chance to revisit what you’ve collected, remember where it came from, and decide whether it still fits your current life. Some items will absolutely stay. Others may have done their job already, even if that job was simply being part of a good memory.


It can also make everyday life easier. A closet with clothes you actually wear, a kitchen drawer without five versions of the same utensil, or a[guest room](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/organizing/how-to-declutter-your-spare-room-for-holiday-guests.html) with room for an actual guest can be a nice change.


### Questions to Ask When Swedish Death Cleaning


Swedish death cleaning can bring up more questions than a typical decluttering session, especially when an item has a memory attached to it. As you sort through your belongings, try asking yourself:


- Do I use or enjoy this now?
- If I saw this in a store today, would I bring it home again?
- Does this item have a story I’d rather write down, photograph, or share with someone?
- Would someone I care about enjoy having it now?
- Is this taking up space because I love it, or because I haven’t decided what to do with it yet?
- Can this move to a “not today” box while I think about it?


## How to Start Swedish Death Cleaning


Swedish death cleaning works best as an ongoing process. You don’t have to pull everything out of every closet or turn your living room into a sorting station.


Choose one drawer, shelf, box, or category. Keep the scope small enough that you can see where the project ends.


### Give Each Item a Next Step


**Next Step** **What It Means**


Keep nearby You use it, enjoy it, or have a clear reason to keep it accessible


Give away or donate Someone else could use it now


Recycle or dispose of locally It’s worn out, broken, or no longer usable


Put away for later use It still fits your life but doesn’t take part in your everyday routine


Not today You want more time before deciding


This approach helps keep a decluttering session from becoming a pile of half-made decisions.


## What Should You Declutter First?


The best first category is usually not the box of family photos or handwritten letters from college. Start with the easy stuff.


Think extra mugs, duplicate kitchen tools, old magazines, clothes that no longer fit your style, and décor you’ve stopped noticing. This is also a great time to meet the mystery cables, unmatched containers, and “maybe I’ll use this someday” supplies that have been quietly living in a drawer for years.


**Start Here** **Why It Works**


Extra dishes, mugs, and kitchen tools Duplicates are easier to spot


Clothing you haven’t worn in a long time Your current routine offers useful clues


Old magazines and duplicate books Clear categories with a natural endpoint


Unused décor Helps you notice what you still enjoy seeing


Hobby materials from old projects Shows which interests still fit your life


Extra towels, linens, or household items Often easier to sort than sentimental belongings


Starting with ordinary items gives you time to practice making decisions before you get to the categories that carry more history.


## How to Handle Sentimental Items


Sentimental belongings can take longer to consider, and that’s completely normal. Sometimes the hardest part of letting something go is the memory attached to it.


### Keep the Memory, Not Every Item


Maybe a vase reminds you of your first apartment. Maybe a stack of postcards brings back a favorite trip. Maybe an old recipe card makes you think of someone you love. You can keep the story without asking every object connected to it to stay forever.


If you’re passing something along to a friend or family member, share the story with it. Add a note, take a photo, or tell them why it mattered to you. That context can mean more than leaving someone to wonder why a particular item was tucked in the back of a closet.


### Create a “Not Today” Box


Some things require more thought than you have available on a Sunday afternoon. That’s where a “not today” box comes in.


Put items you aren’t ready to decide about into one clearly labeled box, then revisit it in a few months. By then, the answer may be clearer. You may want the item nearby, want to share it with someone, or realize you haven’t thought about it once.


Keep this box small. It’s a pause button, not a new permanent category.


### Swedish Death Cleaning vs. Minimalism


**Swedish Death Cleaning** **Minimalism**


Focuses on gradually reviewing belongings over time Focuses on reducing excess and simplifying daily life


Leaves room for stories, memory, and personal context Often emphasizes visual simplicity or fewer possessions


Encourages thoughtful decisions about what stays and what can move on Can range from a less cluttered home to owning fewer items


Has no universal rule for how much someone should own Has no universal rule for how much someone should own


Both approaches can make a home feel less crowded. Swedish death cleaning simply spends more time on the stories behind belongings and what happens to them next.


## Make an Afternoon of It


Swedish death cleaning doesn’t have to be quiet, serious, or solitary. Put on an album. Make a snack. Invite over the friend who can gently ask why you’re still keeping the fondue set you only used once.


You can also give the process a practical payoff. Clear a shelf for books you want to display. Open up a spare room for guests or hobbies.[Tidy a closet](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/organizing/how-to-declutter-your-closet-in-6-easy-steps.html) so getting dressed involves fewer “Where is that?” moments.


The idea is to make your home easier to enjoy now, while the stories are still yours to tell.


## FAQs About Swedish Death Cleaning


**What is Swedish death cleaning?**


Swedish death cleaning, or *döstädning* , is a gradual decluttering practice focused on reviewing belongings, keeping what still fits your life, and letting go of excess over time.


**What does döstädning mean?**


*Döstädning* combines the Swedish words for death and cleaning. It describes thoughtfully sorting through belongings over time.


**Is Swedish death cleaning only for older adults?**


No. Swedish death cleaning can help at many stages of adulthood, including during a move, home update, downsizing project, or household transition.


**What should I declutter first when Swedish death cleaning?**


Start with easy categories, such as unused kitchen items, older clothing, duplicate books, old cables, or décor you no longer enjoy seeing. Save more sentimental belongings for later.


**Is Swedish death cleaning the same as minimalism?**


Not exactly. Both can reduce clutter, but Swedish death cleaning places more focus on personal history and deciding what still belongs in your life.


**Does Swedish death cleaning mean getting rid of everything?**


No. It’s about keeping the belongings that still fit your life and making thoughtful choices about the rest. A home can remain comfortable, personal, and full of things you enjoy.


## A Lighter Way to Look Around Your Home


Swedish death cleaning has a serious name, but it can be a warm, thoughtful practice. It gives you time to enjoy what you keep, share what may bring someone else joy, and let go of the things that have outstayed their welcome.


Start with one uncomplicated category, put on something you like to listen to, and see what you’re ready to pass along.
